unit.title: Crypto basics
unit.description: Blockchain, Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins, wallets and the EU's MiCA regulation

texts: The flatshare accounts
Leo
Irene
Four flatmates keep a list of shared expenses. Each of them keeps a copy of the list.
Well, my copy says I paid for the March shopping.
The other three copies say I paid for it.
Which list counts?
Leo's: it's his copy
A single copy doesn't get the final say. If it doesn't match the others, it's rejected.
The one that matches most of the copies
That's a **blockchain**! Thousands of computers with the same copy of the record.
Let a notary decide
That would work, but the whole point is not needing a middleman.
To sneak a change through you'd need to control most of the network. On Bitcoin, that's hugely expensive.
Does a blockchain do that?
A **blockchain** is a record of transactions shared by thousands of computers (**nodes**). What does it do, and what doesn't it?
Yes, it does
No, it doesn't
Record who sends what to whom
That's its job: a record of transactions.
Guarantee the price goes up
A blockchain protects the record, not the price.
Keep copies on thousands of computers
Each node keeps a copy: nobody controls it on their own.
Give you your money back if you send it to the wrong address
What's recorded can't be undone: your mistakes included.
Let anyone verify the transactions
On a public blockchain, the record is there for everyone to see.
Protect you like a deposit guarantee scheme
No guarantee scheme covers cryptocurrencies.
Sort all six cards.
A blockchain records who owns what **without a middleman**. It doesn't make an asset worth more: cryptos are very volatile and **you can lose everything you invest**.
Hint: it protects the record, not your money.
Sort each card

steps.title: Why it can't be rewritten
steps.body:
Transactions are grouped into **blocks**. Each block carries a fingerprint (**hash**) of the previous one: that's how they're chained together.

If someone changes an old transaction, that block's fingerprint changes and every block after it breaks. On top of that, the other nodes have the correct copy and reject the fake one.
steps.key: Blockchain: a shared, chained record that nobody can rewrite on their own.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for Bitcoin and add it to Favourites to follow it this week.

texts: Live through bitcoin from 2021 to 2025
December 2020: you invest **€1,000** in bitcoin and live through it week by week, with **real data** (in dollars, ignoring the exchange rate). You can sell whenever you like.
Get to the end, whether you sell or not.

In 2021 it nearly doubled in value; from that peak it fell **75 %** by November 2022, and then recovered. That's **extreme volatility**: the past guarantees nothing and you can lose everything you invest.
You've sold. See what happens next…
Down more than 40 %. Can you hold on?
Way up… but what if it turns now?
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
«Digital gold»
Nico
Bitcoin is digital gold: there'll never be more than 21 million.
So it can't drop much, right?
What do you tell him?
Of course: it's scarce, like gold
Scarce isn't the same as stable: you've just seen a 75 % fall.
Its supply is limited, but its price depends on demand
That's it! There are no profits or interest behind it: it's worth what others will pay.
It only drops when there's a halving
No: the halving slows down issuance, but the price moves with demand.
Bitcoin has fallen more than 70 % several times.

steps.title: The halving
steps.body:
Bitcoin was born in 2009, created by someone using the pseudonym **Satoshi Nakamoto**. New bitcoins are created as a reward for whoever adds blocks (the miners). Every **210,000 blocks**, about **4 years**, that reward is cut in half: that's the **halving**.

50 → 25 (2012) → 12.5 (2016) → 6.25 (2020) → **3.125** (2024). After the 2024 halving, 93.75 % of all bitcoins had already been issued.
steps.key: Bitcoin: a maximum of 21 million, with new issuance halving roughly every 4 years.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for Bitcoin and see how far it has fallen from its peak.

texts: Mine from your phone
Laura
Look at this ad: «Mine bitcoins from your phone and earn €50 a day».
Shall I download the app?
What do you tell her?
Yes, it's easy money
Real mining uses specialised machines and loads of electricity. A phone can't compete.
It's almost certainly a scam: a phone can't compete
Nice! Lots of «mining apps» are scams or use your phone for other things.
Install it just to try it out
These apps can expose your data or your wallet. Better not.
When a promise doesn't fit with how the technology works, be suspicious.
Work or stake?
Two ways to decide who adds the next block: **spending energy** on calculations or **putting coins at risk** as collateral. Which is which?
Proof of work
Proof of stake
Bitcoin
Miners compete by spending energy on calculations.
Ethereum, since 2022
It dropped mining in 2022: people who lock up ETH do the validating.
Validated by people who lock up their coins as collateral
That's proof of stake.
Specialised machines trying combinations non-stop
You have to hit a valid hash: there are no shortcuts.
Uses over 99 % less energy
It doesn't need a computing race.
Attacking it takes more power than all the miners combined
The energy spent is what protects the record.
Sort all six cards.
Bitcoin uses **proof of work**: it burns a lot of energy, and that makes attacking it hugely expensive. In 2022 Ethereum switched to **proof of stake**.
Hint: does it burn electricity or put coins at risk?
Sort each card

steps.title: A computing race
steps.body:
**Miners** group transactions into a block and race to find a number that makes its hash meet a condition. The first one collects the **reward** plus the **fees**. Finding the solution costs a lot; checking it, very little.

The **difficulty** adjusts every 2,016 blocks so that a block is found every **10 minutes** on average. And the technology doesn't change the price risk: in crypto **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Proof of work: you earn the right to add blocks by spending energy on calculations.
steps.tip: Try it: create a price alert on Bitcoin and see how much it moves this week.

texts: Free tokens
Unknown website
Congratulations! You've got 500 free tokens waiting for you.
Connect your wallet and sign this contract to claim them.
What do you do?
I sign: it's free
Signing a contract you don't understand can give permission to empty your wallet.
I don't sign anything I don't understand, and I check the project through its official channels
Nice! Lots of scams use smart contract signatures to steal.
I sign with my main wallet, to get more
If it's a trap, you'll lose everything in that wallet.
In a smart contract, code is law… even when it has a bug.
Bitcoin or Ethereum?
**Ethereum** (2015) is a blockchain that, as well as sending money, runs programs; its currency is **ether (ETH)**. Is it Bitcoin or Ethereum?
Bitcoin
Ethereum
There'll never be more than 21 million
It's Bitcoin's headline rule.
Runs smart contracts
Programs that run on their own, with no middleman.
Lending and trading without a bank (DeFi)
They're built with smart contracts on Ethereum.
People call it «digital gold»
Because of its programmed scarcity.
Every transaction pays «gas», which goes up when the network is congested
Gas is paid in ether (ETH).
Digital certificates of ownership (NFTs)
Another thing built on top of Ethereum, like many tokens.
Sort all six cards.
Bitcoin does one thing: **scarce money**. Ethereum is a **platform**: its smart contracts are an «if this happens, do that» that runs on its own.
Hint: Bitcoin is money; Ethereum, a platform for programs.
Sort each card

steps.title: More possibilities, more risks
steps.body:
More features also mean more ways to fail: a bug in a contract's code can let someone drain it, and on a blockchain there's nobody to complain to.

ETH is very volatile and **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Ethereum adds to Bitcoin the ability to run programs: smart contracts.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for Ethereum and compare its chart with Bitcoin's.

texts: The «stable» 20 %
Bruno
May 2022. Bruno has his savings in UST, a stablecoin that tries to always be worth 1 dollar.
A platform pays me nearly 20 % a year to keep them there. And it's stable!
Suddenly, UST starts trading at $0.95.
Is it time to buy more?
What do you tell him?
Yes: buy more, it'll go back to $1
Within days, UST sank far below $1. It never recovered.
That «risk-free» 20 % was hiding a huge risk
That's it: UST lost its peg and LUNA fell almost to zero within days.
Sit tight: they always go back to $1
Some do; UST didn't. «Stable» is a goal, not a guarantee.
Lots of people lost almost everything. High returns «with no risk» don't exist.
Reserve-backed or algorithmic?
A **stablecoin** tries to always be worth the same as a currency, usually **1 dollar**, and there are two ways of trying. Which is which?
Reserve-backed
Algorithmic
Holds dollars and Treasury bills for every token
Its value depends on those reserves existing and being available.
Propped up by another crypto and an algorithm
No real reserves: if confidence breaks, it can spiral down.
TerraUSD (UST), May 2022
It collapsed and dragged LUNA almost to zero.
USDC, March 2023: drops to around $0.87
A bank holding part of its reserves went bust. It got its peg back within a few days.
USDT (Tether)
Like USDC, it backs its tokens with reserves.
Sort all five cards.
Reserve-backed ones depend on **the backing existing** and being available; algorithmic ones, only on **confidence** in the mechanism.
Hint: is there real money behind it, or just a mechanism?
Sort each card

steps.title: What MiCA requires
steps.body:
Stablecoins are used to move between cryptos without going through a bank and to make payments. The most widely used are **USDT** (Tether) and **USDC** (Circle).

In the EU, the **MiCA** regulation requires their issuers to be authorised, hold sufficient, segregated **reserves** and let you **redeem** tokens at par. Even so, «stable» doesn't mean «guaranteed»: they're not covered by the deposit guarantee scheme and **you can lose what you invest**.
steps.key: A stablecoin is worth what its reserves are worth, plus trust in its issuer.
steps.tip: If someone offers you a «stable» 20%, ask your tutor Lumi first.

texts: Can you show it?
You've just created your first **wallet**, the app that holds the **keys** to your crypto. Everyone asks you for something: what can you show without a problem, and what never?
No problem
Never
Your public address, so people can pay you
It's like your IBAN: it's for receiving, not for taking money out.
Your private key
It signs transfers: whoever has it controls the money.
Your seed phrase, to «tech support»
No legitimate party will ever ask you for it.
A photo of your seed phrase, saved in the cloud
Anything connected to the internet can be stolen or leaked.
The record of a transaction, to prove a payment
On a public blockchain, transactions are there for everyone to see.
Your seed phrase, to a friend to keep safe for you
Whoever has it can take everything, with no going back.
Sort all six cards.
Your **address** is shared like an IBAN. Your **private key** and **seed phrase** (12 or 24 words that recover all your keys), never: whoever has them controls your crypto.
Hint: is it for receiving, or for moving your money?
Sort each card
«Tech support»
Tech support
Ana keeps her crypto in self-custody. She gets a message on Telegram.
Hi, Ana. We've detected a fault in your wallet.
To protect your funds, validate your seed phrase on this form. It's urgent.
What does Ana do?
Fill in the form quickly, so she doesn't lose anything
She's just handed over her money: with the phrase, they empty her wallet in minutes.
Ignore the message: no legitimate support team asks for your seed phrase
Nice! It's one of the most common scams in crypto.
Send only half the words
No part of it gets shared. And whoever's asking will keep pushing until they have the rest.
Anyone asking for your seed phrase is robbing you.

steps.title: Your own custody or someone else's
steps.body:
• **On an exchange:** it holds the keys. Convenient, but if it goes bust or freezes your account, you're at its mercy (FTX, 2022).
• **Self-custody:** you hold the keys, in a software or hardware wallet. Nobody can freeze them… but if you lose your seed phrase, **nobody** can recover them.

Your seed phrase goes **on paper or metal, offline**, somewhere safe. Never in a photo, an email or the cloud.
steps.key: «Not your keys, not your coins»: whoever controls the keys controls the crypto.
steps.tip: Ask your tutor Lumi what the difference is between your address and your private key.

texts: An exchange with a freebie
Marta
I've found an exchange with super-low fees and a welcome bonus!
The platform doesn't appear in the CNMV or ESMA registers.
What do you advise her?
Use it: fees are what matter most
Without authorisation, nobody checks whether it keeps your crypto separate or how it uses it.
Look for an authorised provider, even if it charges a bit more
Nice! First, make sure it's supervised; then, that it's cheap.
Deposit a little, to try it out
Even if it's a little, you could lose it with nobody to complain to.
Same as with a broker: first who supervises it, then how much it charges.
Does MiCA protect you?
An **exchange** is a platform for buying and selling crypto, and it almost always holds it for you; the EU's **MiCA** regulation requires it to be authorised. What does it protect you from?
Protects or reduces it
Doesn't protect it
The exchange mixing your crypto with its own
MiCA forces it to keep clients' crypto separate from its own.
A 70 % price crash
MiCA regulates companies, not crypto prices.
The platform not telling you its risks
It requires clear information and a complaints procedure.
Losing your seed phrase in self-custody
Your own mistakes aren't covered by its protection.
An unauthorised platform operating in Spain
According to the CNMV, from 1 July 2026 only authorised providers can operate.
Getting back what you lost if your crypto drops
There's no guarantee scheme for crypto prices.
Sort all six cards.
MiCA reduces the risk of **the platform** misusing your money. The price and your own mistakes are still **your risk**: you can lose everything you invest.
Hint: MiCA supervises companies, not the price.
Sort each card

steps.title: What MiCA requires of them
steps.body:
• **Authorisation** from a national supervisor (in Spain, the CNMV), valid across the EU.
• **Keeping** clients' crypto separate from their own.
• **Capital**, governance and conflict-of-interest requirements.
• Clear information and a **complaints** procedure.

According to the CNMV, from **1 July 2026** only authorised providers can operate in Spain. Before opening an account, look it up in the **CNMV** or **ESMA** registers.
steps.key: MiCA requires exchanges in the EU to be authorised, keep client assets separate and be transparent.
steps.tip: Before opening an account on a real exchange, ask your tutor Lumi how to check it.

u12l1-1.prompt: Put in order how a transaction is recorded on a blockchain.
options: It's grouped with others into a block
The block is added to the chain and everyone updates their copy
The nodes check you have the balance
You send the transaction to the network
u12l1-1.explanation: Check, group, chain and copy: that way nobody needs to trust a middleman.

u12l1-2.prompt: Who controls a public blockchain like Bitcoin's?
options: Nobody on their own: thousands of nodes share the record
u12l1-2.explanation: That's its key feature: the record is spread across many participants.

u12l1-4.prompt: Each block stores the fingerprint, or ____, of the previous block.
u12l1-4.explanation: A hash is a digital fingerprint: change a single piece of data and it changes completely.

u12l1-5.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u12l1-5.explanation: These are the four basic pieces of any blockchain.

u12l1-7.prompt: What does a public blockchain achieve? Select all.
options: Makes rewriting the past very hard
Stops the crypto's price from falling
A record with no central middleman
u12l1-7.explanation: A blockchain protects the record, not the price.

u12l1-9.prompt: Pablo reads in an ad: «Token X, powered by blockchain technology: a 100 % safe investment». What does he think?
options: That blockchain guarantees nothing about value, and «100 % safe» is a red flag
That he has to invest now, before it goes up
If it uses blockchain, it's safe
u12l1-9.explanation: Using technical jargon to promise safety is a common scam tactic.
feedback: Good: blockchain doesn't protect you from the price or from fraud; no serious party promises total safety.
Being rushed is another classic red flag.
Blockchain records transactions; it doesn't protect you from the price or from the project being a fraud.

u12l2-1.prompt: What's the maximum number of bitcoins that can ever exist?
u12l2-1.explanation: It's set in the protocol: issuance slows down with each halving.

u12l2-2.prompt: About every 4 years, Bitcoin's block reward is cut in half: that's the ____.

u12l2-3.prompt: Put Bitcoin's block reward in order over time.
u12l2-3.explanation: Each halving divides the reward by two: issuance slows until it reaches 21 million.

u12l2-6.prompt: This is a chart of one of the big cryptocurrencies, in daily candlesticks. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u12l2-6.explanation: In crypto, a few weeks can bring double-digit moves in either direction: that's why people talk about extreme volatility.

options: What others are willing to pay for it
u12l2-10.explanation: It doesn't generate profits or interest: its price depends on adoption and demand.

u12l2-11.prompt: Bitcoin has been falling for weeks. Nico owns a little and reads on social media: «After every halving it always goes up, put in everything you can». What does he do?
options: He puts in all his savings: the halving guarantees it
He sticks to his plan: he only puts in what he could lose entirely, whatever happens with the halving
He sells everything because, if it falls, Bitcoin must be dead
u12l2-11.explanation: The right one is to follow a plan with an amount you can afford to lose. «It always goes up» mistakes programmed scarcity for a guaranteed price.
feedback: The halving only slows the issuance of new bitcoins. The price depends on demand, and it has fallen more than 70% several times.
Good: scarcity doesn't guarantee the price; what people are willing to pay decides it.
Deciding out of a few weeks of fear is as risky as deciding out of euphoria.

u12l3-1.prompt: Put in order how a Bitcoin block is mined.
options: Tries combinations until it hits a valid hash
The block is added and the miner collects the reward and fees
The network checks the block is correct
u12l3-1.explanation: Finding the solution costs a lot; checking it, very little: that asymmetry is the basis of proof of work.

u12l3-2.prompt: What do miners earn for adding a block?
options: New bitcoins and the transaction fees
A salary from the central bank
u12l3-2.explanation: With each halving the reward drops, so fees will matter more and more.

u12l3-5.prompt: Match each concept to its meaning.
u12l3-5.explanation: Two ways of deciding who adds the next block: by spending energy or by putting coins at risk.
right: How hard it is to find a valid block
Validating by putting up coins as collateral
Validating by spending energy on calculations

u12l3-6.prompt: Ethereum gave up mining in 2022 and moved to proof of ____.
u12l3-6.explanation: Proof of stake: validation is done by those who lock up ETH as collateral.

u12l3-10.prompt: What's true about proof of work? Select all.
options: It makes attacking the network very expensive
Miners compete to solve a calculation
It uses a lot of electricity
u12l3-10.explanation: Ethereum dropped it in 2022 and moved to proof of stake.

u12l3-11.prompt: An acquaintance offers Leo a «cloud mining plan»: he pays a fee and earns a fixed 2% a day, without doing anything. What does Leo think?
options: That it's an easy way to mine without machines
That he'll try it with a little, just in case
That a fixed return doesn't fit real mining, and that it's a clear sign of a scam
u12l3-11.explanation: The right one works because mining doesn't give a fixed return: it depends on the price, the difficulty and the competition. Trying with a little still means giving money to a possible fraud.
feedback: What a real miner earns changes every day: it depends on the price, the difficulty and the fees.
If it's a scam, that little is lost entirely and there's nobody to complain to.
Good: a miner earns the reward and fees only by winning the competition. Nobody serious can promise a fixed 2% a day.

u12l4-1.prompt: Match each concept to its meaning.
u12l4-1.explanation: The basic vocabulary for understanding what goes on inside Ethereum.
right: Program that runs by itself on the blockchain

u12l4-2.prompt: Match each item to what defines it.
u12l4-2.explanation: Bitcoin and Ethereum are separate networks; stablecoins and NFTs are things built on top.
right: Token that tries to always be worth 1 dollar or 1 euro

u12l4-3.prompt: What does Ethereum add to what Bitcoin does?
options: Running programs (smart contracts) on the blockchain
u12l4-3.explanation: That's why tokens, DeFi and NFTs are built on Ethereum.

u12l4-6.prompt: Is it a common use of Ethereum?
options: Protecting your crypto like a deposit guarantee scheme
u12l4-6.explanation: Ethereum makes lots of things possible, but none of them guarantees returns or protects your money like a deposit.

u12l4-9.prompt: Programs that run by themselves on Ethereum are called ____ contracts.
u12l4-9.explanation: Smart contracts: they run when their conditions are met, with no middleman.

u12l4-11.prompt: Irene wants to send some tokens and is in no hurry. Her wallet warns that gas is very expensive today because the network is congested. What does she do?
options: She sends them now: gas is a fixed fee
She sends them over Bitcoin to avoid paying gas
She waits for a moment when the network is calmer
u12l4-11.explanation: The right one works because gas rises and falls with demand on the network. Gas isn't a fixed fee but a price that changes.
feedback: Gas isn't fixed: it rises when the network is congested and falls when demand is low.
Ethereum tokens live on Ethereum: they can't be sent over the Bitcoin network.
Good: with no rush, waiting usually makes the fee much cheaper.

u12l5-1.prompt: What does a stablecoin try to do?
options: Always be worth the same as a currency, like 1 dollar
u12l5-1.explanation: Its goal is stability against a currency, not growth.

u12l5-2.prompt: Match each case or concept to its meaning.
u12l5-2.explanation: Two real episodes that show both risks: no reserves, and reserves in trouble.
right: Fell to around 0.87 $ when a bank collapsed
Swapping 1 token for 1 dollar or 1 euro
Cash and debt backing each token

u12l5-4.prompt: An algorithmic stablecoin has no real reserves backing it.
u12l5-4.explanation: It relies on a mechanism involving another crypto; if confidence breaks, it can spiral down.

u12l5-6.prompt: What does MiCA require of stablecoin issuers in the EU? Select all.
u12l5-6.explanation: MiCA aims to make sure the token is backed and redeemable, not that it earns anything.

u12l5-9.prompt: In March 2023, the stablecoin ____ fell to around 0.87 $ when a bank holding its reserves collapsed.
u12l5-9.explanation: It regained its peg within a few days, once access to those reserves was secured.

u12l5-10.prompt: What's the main risk of a reserve-backed stablecoin?
options: The reserves not existing, not being available or losing value
u12l5-10.explanation: That's why MiCA requires sufficient, segregated and auditable reserves.

u12l6-1.prompt: Put in order the steps to set up a self-custody wallet safely.
options: Generate it and write the seed phrase down on paper
Keep the paper somewhere safe and offline
Send a small test amount before moving more
Download the wallet from its official website
u12l6-1.explanation: A trusted source, an offline copy of the phrase and a small test before risking more.

u12l6-2.prompt: Select the messages that are scams.
options: I'll send you back double if you send 0.1 ETH to this address 😉
Your wallet has been compromised. Verify your 24 words at this link to protect it.
Saw your problem on the forum. Send me your seed phrase and I'll recover your funds.
Remember: never share your seed phrase with anyone.
New login from another device. If it wasn't you, check your account in the app.
u12l6-2.explanation: No legitimate party asks for your seed phrase, and «I'll send you back double» is a classic. Alerts that point you to your own app without asking for details are normal.

u12l6-3.prompt: What does your seed phrase let you recover?
options: All the keys and crypto in your wallet
u12l6-3.explanation: That's why whoever has it can take everything.

u12l6-4.prompt: Where is it safest to keep your seed phrase?
options: On paper or metal, somewhere safe and offline
In an email you send to yourself
In a photo on your phone
u12l6-4.explanation: Anything connected to the internet can be stolen or leaked.

u12l6-7.prompt: Self-custody or custody on an exchange?
options: If you lose your seed phrase, you lose everything
If the platform goes bust, you may lose access
u12l6-7.explanation: Each option swaps one risk for another: the platform's, or your own mistakes.

u12l6-10.prompt: Match each item to its function.
u12l6-10.explanation: Knowing what each piece does tells you which one you can share (only the address) and which never.
right: Storing keys on an offline device

u12l7-1.prompt: What does MiCA require of an exchange operating in the EU? Select all.
options: Keeping clients' crypto separate from its own
u12l7-1.explanation: MiCA regulates the platform, not the price of crypto.

u12l7-2.prompt: Where do you check whether an exchange is authorised? Select all.
u12l7-2.explanation: Only official registers count: anyone can put a fake badge on their website.

u12l7-3.prompt: According to the CNMV, from 1 July 2026, who can provide crypto-asset services in Spain?
u12l7-3.explanation: That day the transition period in Spain came to an end.

u12l7-5.prompt: A MiCA authorisation granted in another EU country allows a provider to operate in Spain.
u12l7-5.explanation: It works like a European passport: one authorisation is valid across the EU.

u12l7-7.prompt: Match each acronym to its meaning.
u12l7-7.explanation: The acronyms you'll see in any warning about crypto platforms in Europe.

u12l7-9.prompt: The EU regulation governing crypto-asset providers is called ____.
u12l7-9.explanation: Markets in Crypto-Assets. MiFID regulates traditional investment services.
